extracted.intended_audience: general readers, mathematicians, graduate students and educators interested in number theory, mathematical research and education
extracted.subtask_description: A news interview/profile of Yitang Zhang covering his research (analytic number theory), reasons for returning to China, mentoring and teaching philosophy, views on computation/AI in math, and ideas about math education and temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduate student selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Find students genuinely interested in analytic number theory, with solid foundational skills and a willingness to delve deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang seeks students who truly want to work in analytic number theory, have strong basic skills, and are willing to engage intensively; he welcomes students regardless of institution (SYSU or elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentoring style and mentor–student relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat students as friends, discuss problems openly, frequently communicate and engage extensively rather than maintaining rigid formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang emphasizes open, frequent communication to spark intellectual exchanges; if a student's interests shift, the mentor should respect the choice and help with job searches or other support rather than punitive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduate teaching format
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate mathematics courses should be primarily discussion-based: sometimes the instructor presents, other times students analyze and present assigned papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang will lead graduate seminars rather than large undergraduate lectures; he assigns papers for students to analyze and present, promoting discussion and deep engagement with material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional requirements for mathematical research
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical research requires minimal physical conditions; any institution with a solid foundation and the freedom to focus is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of institution should prioritize a solid institutional base and academic freedom to concentrate on work, rather than expensive infrastructure or large labs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computers in mathematical research
rubrics_metrics.description: Computers are primarily auxiliary tools for communication, writing, printing and certain calculations; they help but do not replace human reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang uses e-mail and calculation software for tasks like matrix computations; he cites the Four Color Theorem as an example where heavy computation was essential (1200 hours of computer time), but stresses that computers cannot yet replace humans in all proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to AI in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious/skeptical about claims that AI has fully solved major mathematical conjectures; AI may develop further but current evidence is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang has not seen convincing reports that an AI solved the Twin Prime Conjecture and personally is skeptical that AI can fully crack such problems now, though he allows he could be wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work ethic and scholarly temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize solid, painstaking work; avoid impetuosity, exaggeration, and empty boasts about revolutionary results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang advises steady effort, discourages rushing to claim major breakthroughs, and suggests awards should be natural outcomes of sustained improvement rather than primary goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing problem-solving mindset vs. competition training
rubrics_metrics.description: To turn IMO-style competition winners into research mathematicians, help them break free from the 'correct answers' exam mindset and encourage open-ended exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In competitions students learn to produce 'correct answers' and avoid mistakes; research requires attempting conjectures without pre-judgment—mentorship by established mathematicians is key to this transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical literacy for other disciplines
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers in other fields should strengthen their mathematical foundations to avoid incorrect methodologies (e.g., mistaking extensive computational verification for proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang recounts an example of an engineer who verified a formula for billions of values by computer but missed a simple induction proof; this illustrates the need for conceptual mathematical tools in other disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of core curriculum (mathematical induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain foundational topics in school curricula (e.g., mathematical induction) rather than removing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang opposes attempts to remove induction from high-school textbooks, arguing that basic mathematics education relates to the nation's foundational quality and scientific rejuvenation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament traits valuable for mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Calmness, the ability to delve deeply, perseverance and enjoyment of meticulous solitary work are important traits for a practicing mathematician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang cites his own calmness and absorption in interests as conducive to mathematics; such temperament may be innate but is significant for deep, sustained mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality over quantity in mathematical research workforce
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply increasing the number of researchers does not solve deep mathematical problems; careful, concentrated work by capable individuals matters more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zhang rejects the idea that gathering more people (or top teachers) will automatically solve hard problems; mathematics often advances through meticulous individual or small-group effort.
